# Prerequisites

#### Listing 1

Code to install the adatutor package from GitHub, load and attach it.

```{r listing-1}
# Load package
library(remotes)

# Install package from GitHub
# install_github("sbissantz/adatutor")

```

# Empirical Example

#### Listing 2

Code to load the dataset.

```{r listing-2}
# Load data
data(altmext)
```

#### Listing 3

Code to prepare the data.

```{r listing-3}
# Reviewer metrics (names)
pred_nms <- c("power.o", "effect_size.o", "n.o", "p_value.o")

# Outcome variable (name)
out_nme <- "replicate"

# Variables of interest
voi_nms <- c(pred_nms, out_nme)

# Shorten 'altmext'
df <- altmext
```

# Module 1: Data Splitting

#### Listing 4

Code to do a 70/30 simple random split.

```{r listing-4}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportion
prop_train <- 0.7

# Number of effects
n_fx <- nrow(df)

# Number of training samples
n_train <- round(n_fx * prop_train)

# Row positions
fx_seq <- seq_len(n_fx)

# Sample from sequence
fx_smpl <- sample(fx_seq, n_train)

# Inclusion indicator
train_ind <- fx_seq %in% fx_smpl

# Training set
train <- df[train_ind, ]

# Test set (as leftover set)
test <- df[!train_ind, ]
```

::: {.callout-important}
The code has changed. It is not identical to what is in the tutorial.
:::

#### Listing 5

Code to do a 70/15/15 simple random split in one pass.

```{r listing-5}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportions, of the whole data
prop <- c(train = 0.70, valid = 0.15, test = 0.15)

# Set sizes, counted from the whole data
n <- round(n_fx * prop)

# Training sample and inclusion indicator
train_smpl <- sample(fx_seq, n[["train"]])
train_ind <- fx_seq %in% train_smpl

# Validation sample and inclusion indicator
valid_smpl <- sample(fx_seq[!train_ind], n[["valid"]])
valid_ind <- fx_seq %in% valid_smpl

# Training set
train <- df[train_ind, ]

# Validation set
valid <- df[valid_ind, ]

# Test set (as rest set)
test <- df[!train_ind & !valid_ind, ]
```

::: {.callout-important}
The code has changed. It is not identical to what is in the tutorial. Need to rewrite the section.
:::

**Side note**: Every count comes from `n_fx`, so `0.15` means fifteen percent of 202 effects. Splitting in two independent steps (as we did earlier) would make the second proportion relative to what remains, and fifteen percent of the whole would then have to be written `0.15 / (1 - 0.70) = 0.5`.

#### Listing 7

Code to do a 70/30 stratified split.

```{r listing-7}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportion
prop_train <- 0.7

# Partition data based on outcome
set_split <- split(df, df$replicate)

# Number of training samples
n_train <- lapply(set_split, function(set) round(nrow(set) * prop_train))

# Training sample, drawn inside each stratum
train_smpl <- mapply(
  function(set, n) sample(set[, "eid"], n),
  set_split,
  n_train
)

# Inclusion indicator
train_ind <- df$eid %in% unlist(train_smpl)

# Combined sets
strat2_diy <- list(
  "train" = df[train_ind, ],
  "test" = df[!train_ind, ]
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
The code has changed. It is not identical to what is in the tutorial
:::

#### Listing 8

Code to do a 70/15/15 stratified split in one pass.

**Note**: Switched from `props`to `prop`

```{r listing-8}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Split proportions, of the whole data
prop <- c(train = 0.70, valid = 0.15, test = 0.15)

# Partition data based on outcome
set_split <- split(df, df$replicate)

# Set sizes per stratum, both counted from the whole data
n_train <- lapply(set_split, function(set) round(nrow(set) * prop[["train"]]))
n_valid <- lapply(set_split, function(set) round(nrow(set) * prop[["valid"]]))

# Training sample, drawn inside each stratum
train_smpl <- mapply(
  function(set, n) sample(set[, "eid"], n),
  set_split,
  n_train
)
train_eid <- unlist(train_smpl)
train_ind <- df$eid %in% train_eid

# Validation sample, drawn from each stratum's effects that are still available
valid_smpl <- mapply(
  function(set, n) sample(setdiff(set[, "eid"], train_eid), n),
  set_split,
  n_valid
)
valid_ind <- df$eid %in% unlist(valid_smpl)

# Combined sets
strat_diy <- list(
  "train" = df[train_ind, ],
  "valid" = df[valid_ind, ],
  "test" = df[!train_ind & !valid_ind, ]
)
```

#### Listing 9

Code to do a 70/30 random and stratified split, with the pre-implemented function of the adatutor package.

```{r listing-9}
# Simple random split (two way)
set.seed(112)
rand_split <- partition(df, prop = 0.7)

# Stratified split (three way)
set.seed(112)
strat_split <- partition(df, prop = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15), strata = "replicate")

# Verification
mapply(identical, strat_diy, strat_split)
```

We recommend the adatutor's partition() function for the explorations and exercises in the tutorial. It validates inputs and is overall more robust than the DIY code above. For instance,

On `altmext`, the listings and the function agree, but not everywhere:
`sample(x, k)` reads a length-one `x` as `1:x`, so a stratum or a remainder
holding a single row silently draws a value that is not in the data -- with a
four-member stratum, on more than half of all seeds. `partition()` samples
positions with `sample.int()` instead and cannot do this, which is the reason to
reach for a maintained implementation -- this one or `rsample`'s -- once you are
past the tutorial's own data.

#### Figure 1 [NEW]

Visualization of the leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGO-CV) process, with the replication projects as the groups. Reading the graph from left to right, the data are first partitioned into seven projects: Many Labs 1 (ML1, 13 studies), the Replication Project Psychology (RPP, 90), Many Labs 3 (ML3, 10), the Experimental Economics Replication Project (EERP, 18), the Social Science Replication Project (SSRP, 21), Many Labs 2 (ML2, 24), and the decision-market replications of Holzmeister et al. [-@holzmeister2024\; HOLZ, 26], 202 studies in all. Row heights are proportional to project size, except that no row is drawn smaller than 6% of the height, so ML3 appears slightly larger than its share. In Iteration 1, the ML1 project is used as the test set and the other six projects for model training. After fitting the model to the training data, its performance is evaluated on the held-out ML1 studies. This is repeated for each of the other projects (Iterations 2--7), yielding a distribution of seven performance estimates. It might be tempting to summarize them with a single number, but the distribution gives the richer picture of how well the model carries over to a new project.

```{r figure-1}
tutplot_logoscheme(
  df$pid,
  levels = c("ml1", "rpp", "ml3", "eerp", "ssrp", "ml2")
)
```

**Important** Holz is excluded, because it becomes the test set later after validation. 

#### Listing 10

Code to do a 70/30 random and stratified split, with the rsample package.

```{r listing-10}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Simple random split
rand_split_pkg <- rsample::initial_split(df, prop = 0.7)
train_pkg <- rsample::training(rand_split_pkg)
test_pkg <- rsample::testing(rand_split_pkg)

# Stratified split
strat_split_pkg <- rsample::initial_split(df, prop = 0.7, strata = "replicate")
train_pkg <- rsample::training(strat_split_pkg)
test_pkg <- rsample::testing(strat_split_pkg)
```

For real work you will outgrow a single split -- cross-validation, bootstraps,
nested resampling -- and at that point the tool to reach for is the `rsample`
package, which the wider tidymodels ecosystem is built around. Its
`initial_split()` does what `partition()` does and takes the same `strata`
argument, so the idea carries over unchanged; what it adds is the two dozen
other resampling schemes you will want next.

::: {.callout-important title="Restore the split before going on"}

Module 1 showed several ways to split. Everything from Module 2 onward is built on the stratified split of Listings 7 and 8. The package ships it, so load it back and the stumps, weights and figures
come out as described. Setting a seed would not be enough on its own: R changed

# Module 2: Classification Stumps

#### Listing 11

Code to retrieve the frequency tables for the outcome variable under the two
power conditions.

```{r listing-11}
# Condition for the split
split_cond <- train$power.o < 0.927

# Studies with power.o < 0.927
table(train$replicate[split_cond])

# Studies with power.o >= 0.927
table(train$replicate[!split_cond])
```

#### Figure 2

Visualization of a classification tree of depth one or, equivalently, a classification stump. The stump was fitted to the training data using two reviewer metrics: the power of the original study and the number of observations. The middle rectangle represents the root node, and the two lower rectangles are the leaf nodes. The power value used to partition the root node is 0.927. The left leaf node contains about 63% of the training data and the right leaf node contains about 37%. The label in each node ("success", "failure") represents the stump's prediction for each study effect in that node. For example, in the left leaf node, the stump predicts that studies with a power of less than 0.927 will fail replication. According to the training data, 62 of the 89 study effects with a power of less than 0.927 actually failed replication.

```{r figure-2}
# Fit classification stump
# Note: Two metrics only
cstump_int <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  maxdepth = 1,
  # keep to recycle below
  model = TRUE
)

# Visualize
tutplot_cstump(cstump_int, extra = 102)
```

#### Listing 12

Code to set the hyperparameters of a classification tree and fit the model to
the training data.

```{r listing-12}
# Fit classification stump
cstump <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  # Classification tree
  method = "class",
  # Maximum depth
  maxdepth = 1,
  # Gini impurity (default)
  parms = list(split = "gini")
)
```

#### Listing 13

Code to visualize a fitted classification stump. `cstump` is the model behind Figure 2: the same two reviewer metrics, splitting on `power.o` at 0.927 into leaves of 89 and 52. It is `cstump_int` with the arguments spelled out, so this listing reproduces that figure. The four-metric stump -- which splits on `p_value.o` at 0.0007 into leaves of 90 and 51 -- is `cstump_fit`, fitted in Listing 24.

```{r listing-13}
# Color-blind pallette
sty <- viridis_tree(cstump)

# Visualize classification stump
cstump |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(
    extra = 100,
    digits = 4,
    box.col = sty$box,
    col = sty$text
  )
```

#### Figure 3

Visualization of the decision boundary of a classification stump. The predictor variable on the x-axis is the power of the original study effect. The predictor variable on the y-axis is the number of observations. So the y-axis does not display the outcome variable, but another study characteristic. However, since classification stumps are classification trees of depth one, only one study characteristic (i.e., power in this case) is used as a predictor to separate successfully replicated study effects from failed ones. The decision boundary is set at a power value of 0.927 (vertical line). The model predicts that any point in the gray region is a successful replication, while anything in the blue region is considered a failure. Gray triangles represent replications of study effects that actually succeeded (i.e., according to the replication metric), while blue circles represent replications that actually failed. Thus, gray triangles in the blue region are misclassifications, and vice versa.

```{r figure-3}
# Visualize
# Note: the stump from Figure 2, now as the boundary it draws
tutplot_boundary(
  cstump_int,
  data = train,
  xlab = "Power (Original Study)",
  ylab = "Sample Size (Original Study)"
)
```

#### Figure 4

Visualization of the Gini impurity for a two-class classification problem. The x-axis is the proportion or probability of Class 1 (e.g., the proportion of successes in the empirical example). The y-axis is the measure of Gini impurity. The Gini impurity is highest when the classes are equally represented. This occurs when the proportion of Class 1 is 0.5, meaning there are as many instances of Class 1 (i.e., successes) as of Class 2 (i.e., failures). The more homogeneous a class becomes, the lower the Gini impurity. The Gini impurity is zero if there are only instances of one type (i.e., only successes or failures).

```{r figure-4}
# Visualize
tutplot_gini(x_seq = seq(0.01, 1, by = 0.01), lwd = 2)
```

#### Listing 14

Code to calculate means of neighboring units and find the position of the
relevant power value.

```{r listing-14}
# Sorted vector
power_srt <- sort(train$power.o)

# Adjacent means
adjmeans <- (power_srt[-1] + power_srt[-length(power_srt)]) / 2

# Find position of value '0.927'
which(round(adjmeans, 4) == 0.927)

# Additional

adj_pat <- which(round(adjmeans, 4) == 0.927)
const <- adjmeans[adj_pat]
N_total <- nrow(train) # 141
criterion_left <- train$power.o < const
N_left <- length(train$replicate[criterion_left]) # 89 total
left_success <- sum(as.numeric(train$replicate[criterion_left]) - 1) # 27
left_failure <- N_left - left_success # 62 failures

# Gini impuritiy (left)
gini_left <- 1 - ((left_failure / N_left)^2 + (left_success / N_left)^2)
gini_left # 0.423
criterion_right <- train$power.o >= const
N_right <- length(train$replicate[criterion_right]) # 52
right_success <- sum(as.numeric(train$replicate[criterion_right]) - 1) # 40
right_failure <- N_right - right_success # 12

# Gini impuritiy (right)
gini_right <- 1 - ((right_failure / N_right)^2 + (right_success / N_right)^2)
gini_right # 0.3550296
# Overall weighted Gini impurity
gini_impurity <- (N_left / N_total) *
  gini_left +
  (N_right / N_total) * gini_right
round(gini_impurity, digits = 5) # 0.39773
# Sorted values
power_srt <- sort(train$power.o)
adjmeans <- (power_srt[-1] + power_srt[-length(power_srt)]) / 2
gini_impurity <- vector(length = length(adjmeans))
for (i in seq_along(adjmeans)) {
  constant <- adjmeans[i]
  N_total <- nrow(train)
  # Left leaf
  criterion_left <- train$power.o < constant
  N_left <- length(train$replicate[criterion_left])
  left_success <- sum(as.numeric(train$replicate[criterion_left]) - 1)
  left_failure <- N_left - left_success
  # Right leaf
  criterion_right <- train$power.o >= constant
  N_right <- length(train$replicate[criterion_right])
  right_success <- sum(as.numeric(train$replicate[criterion_right]) - 1)
  right_failure <- N_right - right_success
  # Gini index
  gini_d1 <- 1 - ((left_failure / N_left)^2 + (left_success / N_left)^2)
  gini_d2 <- 1 - ((right_failure / N_right)^2 + (right_success / N_right)^2)
  # Impurity
  gini_impurity[i] <- (N_left / N_total) *
    gini_d1 +
    (N_right / N_total) * gini_d2
}
# Position of smallest impurity
which.min(gini_impurity)
# Outcome
adjmeans[which.min(gini_impurity)]
```

#### Listing 16

Code to show the sensitivity to observation weights by using normalized random
weights from a uniform distribution.

Visualization of a classification stump fitted with normalized random weights. Note that we simplified the visual output shown here by using the `extra` argument of the `rpart.plot()` function with a value set to `100`.

:::{ .callout-note}
The tutorila says: "one of the p-values", but now the variable doesn't change at all; the threshold does. (power.o < 0.9206, against 0.927 with equal weights)

```{r listing-16}
# For reproducibility
set.seed(112)

# Draws from standard uniform

# Normalize (sum to 1)

  replicate ~ power.o + n.o,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
```

# Module 3: AdaBoost

#### Listing 17

Code to understand the givens in the AdaBoost algorithm.

```{r listing-17}
# Predictors and outcome (names)
pred_nms
out_nme

# Predictor matrix
x_train <- train[, pred_nms]

# Outcome vector
y_train <- train[, out_nme]

# Indices
i <- 1
m <- nrow(train)

# i-th row or element
x_train[i, ]
y_train[i]

# i-th to m-th row (i.e., all)
cbind(x_train, y_train)[i:m, ]
```

#### Listing 18

Code to generate initialization weights in the AdaBoost algorithm.

```{r listing-18}
# Initialization weights
D1 <- rep(1, m) / m
```

#### Listing 19

Code to fit a classification stump with the initialization weights.

```{r listing-19}
# Fit classification stump
h1 <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = 1,
  weights = D1
)
```

#### Listing 20

Code to calculate the classification stump's error.

```{r listing-20}
# Retrodictions (training data)
y_retro <- predict(h1, newdata = train[, voi_nms], type = "class")

# Retrodictive error
epsilon <- sum(D1 * (y_retro != y_train))
```

#### Listing 21

Code to calculate the classification stump's performance.

```{r listing-21}
# Retrodicitve performance
perf <- sum(D1 * (y_retro == y_train))

# Retrodictive error
epsilon <- 1 - perf
```

#### Listing 22

Code to calculate the classification stump's weight assuming a learning rate eta of 1.

```{r listing-22}
# Learning rate
eta <- 1

# Model weight
alpha1 <- 1 / 2 * log(perf / epsilon) * eta
```

#### Figure 6

Visualization of how the importance of a classification stump ($\alpha_t$) varies with its performance ($1-\epsilon_t$). Overall, the better the performance of a stump, the higher its weight. Put another way, the lower a stump's error ($\epsilon_t$), the higher its importance ($a_t$). The boosting hyperparameter ($\eta$) allows to further attenuate the weight of a classification stump. This could later help to improve the predictive performance of AdaBoost (see Module 4).

```{r figure-6}
# Learning rates
eta_int <- c(eta, 0.5, 0.1)

# Visualize
tutplot_importance(eta = eta_int, marked_perf = perf, marked_eta = eta)
```

#### Listing 23

Code to calculate the update factor for the initialization weights.

```{r listing-23}
# Indicator trick
chi1 <- (y_retro == y_train) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train) * -1

# Unnormalized weights
D2_raw <- D1 * exp(-alpha1 * chi1)

# Normalization constant
Z1 <- sum(D2_raw)

# Normalized weights
D2 <- D2_raw / Z1
```

#### Figure 7

Visualization of how the update factor ($e^{-\alpha\chi}$) varies depending on the classification result and the importance of the model ($\alpha_t$). If the classifier classifies an observation correctly, $\chi$ takes the value 1 and the weight or importance of the observation is reduced in the next iteration. In the case of a misclassification, $\chi$ takes the value -1 and the weight of the observation increases. The observation will be more important in the next iteration.

**TODO** I use $a$ as model weight not alpha! Either a or alpha needs fixing. Switch to alpha?

```{r figure-7}
# Model weights: yours in the middle, a heavier and a lighter one either
# side. Taken relative to alpha1, so they follow it if you change eta
alpha_int <- round(alpha1 * c(1.35, 1, 0.6), 3)
# Visualize
# Note: One curve per model weight
tutplot_updatefactor(
  # Model weights
  alpha = alpha_int,
  # Rise figure
  pch = c(20, 17, 15),
  lty = 3,
  lwd = 1,
  ylim = c(0.3, 2.2)
)
```

#### Figure 8

Visualization of the result of the weight updating process after Iteration 1 for the first 25 data points in the `altmext` training set. The gray initial weights $D_1$ increase or decrease depending on whether the first classification stump classified them correctly (green dot in the middle) or not (red dot in the middle). If the stump misclassifies an observation, its weight moves up and becomes larger, i.e., its importance increases. Correctly classified data points experience a weight decrease. They become less important in the next iteration. Visually, they move down and become smaller.

```{r figure-8}
# Visualize
# Note: The band marks the points the first stump missed
tutplot_weightone(d1 = D1, d2 = D2, chi = chi1)
```


#### Listing 24

Code to loop through the algorithmic steps.

::: {.callout-note}
The code can take several seconds to complete.
:::

```{r listing-24}
# Number of trees
T <- 1000

# Learning rate
eta <- 1

# Lists for models and weights
ada_diy <- vector("list", T)

# Initial observation weights
D <- rep(1, m) / m

# Loop through steps
for (t in seq_len(T)) {
  h <- rpart::rpart(
    replicate ~ .,
    data = train[, voi_nms],
    method = "class",
    maxdepth = 1,
    # Turn off, surrogates stand in for missing values, but we have none.
    # Leaving it on would put extra variables into each stump's
    # `variable.importance` and pull the scores below apart.
    maxsurrogate = 0,
    weights = D
  )
  y_retro <- predict(object = h, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "class")
  e <- sum(D * (y_retro != y_train))
  a <- 0.5 * log((1 - e) / e) * eta
  chi <- (y_retro == y_train) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train) * -1
  D_raw <- (D * exp(-a * chi))
  D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)
  ada_diy[[t]] <- list("h" = h, "a" = a)
}
names(ada_diy) <- paste0("t", seq_len(T))

# Show first model weight
cat("Model weight 1:", ada_diy$t1$a)
```

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Code to fit the same ensemble with the adatutor package.

```{r listing-24-pkg}
# Use stump as weak learner
cstump_fit <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  # Tree hyperparameter
  maxdepth = 1,
  # Keep the training data
  model = TRUE,
  parms = list(split = "gini")
)

# Take the stump and boost it
ada_fit <- cstump_fit |> adaboost(n_iter = T, eta = eta)

# Verification
identical(sapply(ada_diy, "[[", "a"), sapply(ada_fit, "[[", "a"))
```

**Add to tutorial**: As both are weight by weight identical, we will use the package solution in the following to save some typing and support readers on their exploraiton of the algorithm with some additional sugar and safe guards we implemented in the package function.

**Add to tutorial**: Furthermore, the signature l. 802 also makes explicit what is often taken for granted: the weak learner is a (classification) stump. In fact the algorithm is written to accept any weak learner, with a performance slighly better than guessing (we see this in Eq. xxx). So the weak learner is iself a choice (a free hyperparameter if you will) and in fact you can also boost other models as well, such as deep trees or single-layer perceptrons (if you want to get wild). That said, `adaboost()` only accepts trees as this tutorial introduced them in Module 2. Indeed, stumps are a convenient choice, especially because of their simplicity and thus explainability which we will discuss next.

**TODO** Remove, keep at a different place?
::: {.callout-tip}
## The tree depth belongs to the tree, not to the boosting

`adaboost()` takes a fitted learner, so there is only one place to set depth:
the `rpart()` call that builds it. Everything in `h$control` is carried into
every round -- `maxdepth`, `cp`, `minsplit`, `minbucket` -- so the tree you
looked at is the tree that gets boosted.

Two controls are overridden, and only those two. `xval` and `maxsurrogate` are
forced to zero: ten internal cross-validations per weak learner that nothing
reads cost about thirty per cent of the runtime, and neither setting changes
the tree that comes out. Everything you chose, you keep.

This is why AdaBoost has no `maxdepth` argument. The algorithm is defined over
*any* weak learner whose weighted error stays below one half; a tree is one
choice among many, and its settings are yours rather than the algorithm's.
:::

## NEW: Feature Importance

In the introduction, we punchily stated that our goal is to turn AdaBoost into a "glass-box" tool for applied work. So far, this meant taking the algorithm apart, inspecting its nuts and bolts, and rebuilding it in code. Now we go one step further and put this knowledge to work. We build a tool that lets us inspect the fitted model and see which predictors the ensemble focuses on as it learns. This is the question of feature importance, part of the wider field of interpretable machine learning (IML). Because this tutorial focuses on AdaBoost, not on IML in general, we will only scratch the surface of what is possible. Specifically, we will develop a model-specific measure for boosted trees. Model-agnostic methods, such as permutation importance and effect plots, go much further and readers who want to learn more can find it in more specialized resources [see, e.g., @molnar2025; @pargent2023].

Most importance measures for tree ensembles build on two quantities: how often a predictor is used to split (split frequency) and how much its splits reduce impurity (gain). For our stumps, we build on the first and weight each split by its stump's model weight. The result is a **relative importance** measure, which gives each predictor's share, in percent, of the model weight of all stumps that split. Two insights from earlier modules make this work: In Module 2 we showed that a stump splits (at most) once, on one predictor, and in Module 3 we taught that each stump carries a model weight `a`, which grows with the stump's accuracy on the weighted data. To get the importance score, we now simply group the stumps by the predictor they split on and sum their model weights. Why does this make sense? Well, AdaBoost shifts weight toward the observations the ensemble still gets wrong (or barely right), so each new stump works on the ensemble's biggest mistakes. A predictor that many stumps choose, especially stumps with high model weights, is one the ensemble relies on again and again for its corrections. The summed weight thus shows how much the ensemble relies on each predictor relative to the others. Listing xxx puts this into code.

```{r importance-frame}
n_preds <- length(pred_nms)
# initialization: vector of zeros
voz <- numeric(n_preds)
imp_diy <- setNames(voz, pred_nms)
for (t in seq_along(ada_diy)) {
  # variable at the root (stumps)
  h <- ada_diy[[t]]$h
  v <- as.character(h$frame$var[1])
  # if it does not split, skip it
  if (v == "<leaf>") {
    next
  }
  imp_diy[v] <- imp_diy[v] + ada_diy[[t]]$a
}
# relative importance: normalize and scale
imp_diy <- imp_diy / sum(imp_diy) * 100
# highest importance first
sort(imp_diy, decreasing = TRUE)
```

First, we start with storing the number of predictiors and initializing a named vector of zeros, one entry per predictor. The loop then starts from that vector and adds each stump's model weight to the entry of the predictor it splits on (`imp_diy[v] <- imp_diy[v] + ada_diy[[t]]$a`).FOOTONOTE The `rpart()` functions stores that predictor in `frame`, which is the tree's table of nodes. Its first row is the root, so for a stump, `frame$var[1]` is the predictor it splits on. A stump may also not split at all; then `frame$var[1]` reads `<leaf>`, and `next` skips it. Finally, we divide by the total and multiply by 100, so the scores sum to 100 and read as percentages.

Errors are then far more obvious then with hidden partial matches often easier to debug. We keep it here since most readers are familiar with the `$` operator and we ensured partical matching does not cause any problems here. In the box in Listing (deep tree importance) we give an example of what we mean.

Footnote: Why would a stump not split? By default, `rpart` only makes a split if it improves the fit by at least the complexity parameter, `cp = 0.01`, that is, 1 percent of the error at the root. With our training data, 97 of the 1,000 stumps found no such split, so we need to skip those cases when implementing it.

The package function `gauge()` computes the measure for trees of any depth (see box below) 
we added a `plot()` function to the adadtutor package, so readers can easily visualize the result.
**TODO**: Make plot function look better :D? 80's barplot.

```{r}
#| label: importance
important <- gauge(ada_fit)
head(important, 10)
imp <- setNames(important$importance, important$variable)
identical(imp, imp_diy[names(imp)])
# visualize
important |> plot(top_n = 15)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Deeper trees: split frequency meets gain

Deeper trees can split on several predictors. Then each tree's model weight is shared among the predictors it uses, in proportion to how much each one's splits reduce impurity (gain). In our case, the impurity is the Gini impurity of Module 2. The measure becomes a mix: the model weight decides how much a tree counts, and the gain decides how its share is divided. This is a weighted version of the mean decrease in impurity. In code, one line changes: `share <- ada_deep[[t]]$a * vi / sum(vi)`.

```{r importance-general}
# Fit the weak learner: a depth-4 tree, not a stump
ada_deep <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  # going deep
  maxdepth = 4,
  model = TRUE
) |>
  adaboost(n_iter = 10, eta = 1)

imp_deep <- setNames(voz, pred_nms)
for (t in seq_along(ada_deep)) {
  # rpart()'s built-in vi measure
  h <- ada_deep[[t]][["h"]]
  vi <- h[["variable.importance"]]
  if (is.null(vi)) {
    next
  }
  # Split the weight across the variables this tree used,
  # in proportion to each split's improvement
  share <- ada_deep[[t]][["a"]] * vi / sum(vi)
  imp_deep[names(share)] <- imp_deep[names(share)] + share
}
imp_deep <- 100 * imp_deep / sum(imp_deep)
sort(imp_deep, decreasing = TRUE)
```

Why do stumps lose the gain? In the line above, a stump's `vi` holds one number, so `vi / sum(vi)` is always 1. The gain still decides which predictor a stump picks, but not how much weight that predictor gets. The `gauge()` function in the `adatutor` package runs the general version, which is why it matches the stump loops exactly.
:::

#### Figure 9

Visualization of the decision boundary of 1000 adaptively boosted shallow classification trees. The number of trees matches the Listings 24 and 25, but the trees were fitted to the training data using only two reviewer metrics: the power of the original study and the number of observations. The x-axis is the power of the original study effect. The y-axis is the number of observations. Note that the y-axis is not the outcome variable, but another study characteristic. The model predicts that any point in the gray region is a successful replication, while anything in the blue region is considered a failure. Gray triangles represent replications of study effects that actually succeeded (i.e., according to the replication metric), while blue circles represent replications that actually failed. Thus, gray triangles in the blue region are misclassifications, and vice versa.

```{r figure-9}
tutplot_boundary(
  ada_int,
  data = train,
  xlab = "Power (Original Study)",
  ylab = "Sample Size (Original Study)"
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## `type = "class"` gives balanced accuracy, not AUC

A two-valued score collapses the ROC curve to a single interior point, whose
area is exactly (sensitivity + specificity) / 2. Use `type = "margin"` for the
AUC; keep `type = "class"` for the confusion matrix.
:::

## Evaluating Model Performance

#### Listing 31

Code showing different measures to evaluate the predictive performance of the
ensemble.

```{r listing-31}
# Confusion matrix
conf_mat <- table(y_pred_cls, y_test)

# Accuracy
sum(diag(conf_mat)) / sum(conf_mat)

# Balanced Accuracy
auroc(y_test, y_pred_cls)

# Area under the curve (scored on the margin)
auroc(y_test, y_pred_mgn)

# Other metrics
assess(y_test, score = y_pred_mgn)

# Base rates
df$replicate_ind <- as.integer(df$replicate) - 1
baserate <- aggregate(replicate_ind ~ pid, df, mean)

# Average base rate
mean(baserate$replicate_ind)
```

**Note on margins**: A hard label can only ever be right or wrong. The margin says how confidently (unnormalized), and every measure that reads a ranking needs that. Keep it in mind for Module 4, where the cross-validation scores on the margin throughout.

::: {.callout-important}
## Switched to `PRROC` package
Cite and fix everywhere - especially in the tutorial.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
`auroc()` is a thin wrapper around `PRROC::roc.curve()` (Grau, Grosse &
Keilwagen). Specifically, `auprc()` wraps `pr.curve()`. The wrapper exists so the outcome can be passed in whatever form you have it, for instance as a factor, 0/1, -1/1 or logical. `roc.curve()` itself expects a 0/1 vector and returns a "wrong" number without complaining if you feed it a 1/2.

The precision-recall curve plots `ppv` (precision) against `sens` (recall) over every threshold, just as the ROC curve plots `sens` against 1 - `spec`. See `?assess` for the other names each measure goes by.
:::

## Leave-One-Group-Out Cross-Validation

#### Listing 32

Code to do a leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

::: {.callout-note}
This ran for approximately 2 minutes on our laptops.
:::

```{r listing-32}
# Hold out the newest project, HOLZ (2024), as the final test set
df_holz <- df[df$pid == "holz", ]
df_noholz <- df[df$pid != "holz", ]

# Partition the tuning data by project ID
df_split <- split(df_noholz, df_noholz$pid)
proj_nms <- names(df_split)
# List for AUC results
auc <- list()

runtime <- system.time({
  # LOGO-CV
  for (rp in proj_nms) {
    # for (rp in c("eerp", "ml1", "ml3", "rpp", "ssrp")) {
    message("\nProject: ", paste0(rp), "\n")
    # Training and test set
    test <- df_split[[rp]]
    train <- df_noholz[!(df_noholz$pid %in% rp), ]
    # Fit model to data
    h <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train[, voi_nms],
      maxdepth = 1,
      model = TRUE
    )
    fit <- adaboost(h, n_iter = 1000, eta = 1)
    # Predictions (left-out project), on the margin so the AUC sees the ranking
    y_pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test[, pred_nms], type = "margin")
    # Performance evaluation
    auc[[rp]] <- auroc(test$replicate, y_pred)
  }
})

# Waiting time
message("\n Run time: ", runtime["elapsed"], " s\n")

# Results
c(unlist(auc))
# c(unlist(auc)) |> mean()
```

```{r figure-xx}
# The weak learner, on the six tuning projects: logo_cv() reads only its recipe
h <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms],
  maxdepth = 1,
  model = TRUE
)

# LOGO-CV: refit the same recipe with each project held out
logo_int <- h |>
  adaboost(n_iter = 1000, eta = 1, verbose = FALSE) |>
  logo_cv(data = df_noholz, group = "pid")

# Visualize (manuscript figure)
set.seed(112)
tutplot_logocv(logo_int, n_resample = 500)
```

`logo_cv()` uses the fit's settings, not its data: it refits the same recipe
once per project, holding that project out. The plot shows each project's
estimate and its spread, not a mean. The projects differ in size and share
most of their training data, so an average would hide both.

## Hyperparameter Optimization

#### Listing 33

Code to define a hypergrid.

```{r listing-33}
# Define hypergrid
hgrid <- expand.grid(
  # Tree-specific:
  # Tree depth
  "depth" = 1:3,
  # Boosting specific:
  # Number of trees
  "T" = c(10, 100, 1000),
  # Learning rate
  "eta" = c(1, 0.1)
)

# Container for fold performance, one column per tuning project
proj_nms <- sort(unique(df_noholz$pid))
hgrid[proj_nms] <- NA_real_
hgrid$auc.mean <- NA_real_
hgrid$auc.sd <- NA_real_
hgrid$auc.stable <- NA_real_
hgrid$runtime <- NA_real_
```

#### Optional: Random Search

Instead of trying every setting, a random search tries a few, drawn at random.
It needs one step after Listing 33:

```{r random-search}
# Draw `n_draws` settings at random from the grid
n_draws <- 8
set.seed(112)
hgrid_rnd <- hgrid[sample(nrow(hgrid), n_draws), ]
```

To search only these, use `hgrid_rnd` in place of `hgrid` in Listing 34. With
the package, the drawn rows are simply the grid you hand to `logo_cv()`:

```{r random-search-package}
# LOGO-CV over the drawn settings, on the six tuning projects
logo_rnd <- logo_cv(
  replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o,
  data = df_noholz,
  group = "pid",
  grid = hgrid_rnd[, c("depth", "T", "eta")]
)

# The most stable of the drawn settings (mean minus SD), as in Listing 34
rnd_auc <- logo_rnd$estimates[,, "auroc"]
rnd_stable <- rowMeans(rnd_auc) - apply(rnd_auc, 1, sd)
logo_rnd$grid[which.max(rnd_stable), ]
```

#### Listing 34

Code to do hyperparameter optimization using a leave-one-group-out
cross-validation strategy.

**TODO** Random grid search!
**TODO** Exclude mean AUC? 

::: {.callout-note}
This ran for approximately 3 minutes on our laptops.
:::

```{r listing-34}
# Number of rows
hgrid_rows <- nrow(hgrid)

# Partition the tuning data by project ID
df_split <- split(df_noholz, df_noholz$pid)

# Hyperparameter optimization
for (i in seq_len(hgrid_rows)) {
  # Iteration time
  runtime <- system.time({
    # Leave-one-group-out CV
    for (rp in proj_nms) {
      # Progress report
      cat(
        "\rProgress: ",
        round(i / hgrid_rows * 100),
        "%",
        " | T: ",
        hgrid$T[i],
        " | eta: ",
        hgrid$eta[i],
        " | depth: ",
        hgrid$depth[i],
        " | model: ",
        rp
      )
      # Training and test set
      test <- df_split[[rp]]
      train <- df_noholz[!(df_noholz$pid %in% rp), ]
      # Fit model to data
      h <- rpart::rpart(
        replicate ~ .,
        data = train[, voi_nms],
        maxdepth = hgrid$depth[i],
        model = TRUE
      )
      fit <- adaboost(
        h,
        n_iter = hgrid$T[i],
        eta = hgrid$eta[i],
        verbose = FALSE
      )
      # Predictions (on the margin, so the AUC sees the ranking)
      y_pred <- predict(
        fit,
        newdata = test[, pred_nms],
        type = "margin",
        verbose = FALSE
      )
      # Performance evaluation
      hgrid[[rp]][i] <- auroc(test$replicate, y_pred)
    }
    # Average performance, its spread across projects, and the two combined
    fold_auc <- as.numeric(hgrid[i, proj_nms])
    hgrid$auc.mean[i] <- mean(fold_auc)
    hgrid$auc.sd[i] <- sd(fold_auc)
    hgrid$auc.stable[i] <- hgrid$auc.mean[i] - hgrid$auc.sd[i]
  })
  hgrid$runtime[i] <- runtime[["elapsed"]]
}

# Hypergrid sorted by the most stable performance (mean minus SD)
hgrid[order(-hgrid$auc.stable), ] |> round(2)
```

**NEW**
The mean tells us how well a setting can be expected to do on a new project; the spread tells us how much to trust that expectation. A setting with a high mean and a small spread is the safest bet.

#### Listing [NEW]

Listing 34 searches 18 settings. The package ships a much larger search as `hypergrid`: 2,640 settings (depth 1 to 8, 15 learning rates, and T from 10 to 3,000), each scored by LOGO-CV on the six tuning projects under all 17 measures of `assess()`. HOLZ takes no part, so it stays untouched for the final test. `hypergrid` is a list with one table per measure. Each row is a setting and each project a column. Before summarizing, look at the projects one by one.

```{r hypergrid-projects}
data(hypergrid)

# One table per measure: a row per setting, a column per tuning project
names(hypergrid)
auc <- hypergrid$auroc
proj_nms <- attr(hypergrid, "projects")$project
```

The projects differ far more than the settings do. Over all 2,640 settings, the median AUC is .93 on ML1 but .64 on ML3 and RPP, and RPP, the largest project with 90 studies, never gets above .69. The three settings show the trade-off a summary has to make. The stumps (Listing 34's winner) and the depth-2 trees reach .96 on ML1, while the depth-5 trees give up ML1 (.82) but do better on ML2 and SSRP, so their results vary less across projects. The stability rule of Listing 34 weighs exactly this: a high average against a small spread.

```{r hypergrid-stable}
# Stability as in Listing 34: mean minus SD across the projects
proj_auc <- as.matrix(auc[proj_nms])
auc$auc.mean <- rowMeans(proj_auc)
auc$auc.sd <- apply(proj_auc, 1, sd)
auc$auc.stable <- auc$auc.mean - auc$auc.sd
# The worst project, which we use as a safeguard below
auc$auc.min <- apply(proj_auc, 1, min)
```

Stability is not the only thing we care about. HOLZ is a single new project, so we also want to know how badly a setting can do on one project. Only three settings are not beaten on both counts: no other setting has both a higher stability and a better worst project. The table puts them next to the best stump, the model this tutorial builds.

```{r hypergrid-unbeaten}
# All settings, the most stable first
hypar_auc <- auc[order(-auc$auc.stable, -auc$auc.min), ]

# (a) depth 1, the stumps of this tutorial: the most stable stump setting
best_d1 <- hypar_auc[hypar_auc$depth == 1, ][1, ]

# (b) the unbeaten settings: down the list sorted by stability, keep a setting
# only if its worst project beats every setting above it
unbeaten <- hypar_auc[
  hypar_auc$auc.min > cummax(c(-Inf, head(hypar_auc$auc.min, -1))),
]

# Settings in rows; the projects, then the summaries, side by side
cols <- c(
  "depth",
  "T",
  "eta",
  proj_nms,
  "auc.mean",
  "auc.sd",
  "auc.stable",
  "auc.min"
)
rbind(best_d1, unbeaten)[cols] |> print(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r hypergrid-safeguard}
# Safeguard against the worst project: the best worst case, ties by stability
best <- auc[order(-auc$auc.min, -auc$auc.stable), ][1, ]
best[c("depth", "T", "eta", "auc.stable", "auc.min")]
```

If we safeguard against the worst project, we pick the setting whose weakest project is strongest and break ties by stability: depth 2, T = 2000, eta = .02. It boosts a weak learner, as AdaBoost intends, and on this criterion it sits on a plateau: from T = 800 to 2500, its worst project stays between .66 and .68. All three would have been a good choice, though: they differ by less than .02 on either measure, well within the noise of six projects. 

**NOTE**: An `NA` here means "undefined" rather than "failed": precision among the top five (`patk_5`) has no value for ML3, which has only three successful replications.

## Finalizing an Ensemble

#### Listing 35

Code to refit the safeguard setting of the hypergrid on the six tuning projects
and test it on HOLZ.

```{r listing-35}
# The safeguard setting from the hypergrid: depth 2, T 2000, eta .02
best[c("depth", "T", "eta")]

# Refit it on all six tuning projects
h_final <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms],
  maxdepth = best$depth,
  model = TRUE
)
fit_final <- adaboost(h_final, n_iter = best$T, eta = best$eta)

# The final test: score it once on HOLZ, on the margin so the AUC sees the
# ranking
y_ada <- predict(fit_final, newdata = df_holz[, pred_nms], type = "margin")
auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_ada)
```

## Benchmarks

Compare the results from ligistic regression, adaboost and decision trees here?

```{r benchmarks}
# Baseline: logistic regression on the same predictors and projects
fit_logit <- glm(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms],
  family = binomial
)

# Baseline: a single tree on the same predictors and projects. Its depth, 5, is
# chosen by the same LOGO-CV rule on the six tuning projects (mean minus SD)
fit_tree <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms],
  maxdepth = 5
)

# Default random forests on the same predictors
set.seed(112)
fit_rf <- randomForest::randomForest(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = df_noholz[, voi_nms]
) # mtry=2, nodesize=1

# Score each baseline once on HOLZ, on its probability of success rather than
# the class, so the AUC sees the ranking
y_logit <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = df_holz, type = "response")
y_tree <- predict(fit_tree, df_holz[, pred_nms], type = "prob")[, "success"]
y_rf <- predict(fit_rf, df_holz[, pred_nms], type = "prob")[, "success"]

# All models on the same 26 HOLZ studies; AdaBoost's score is from Listing 35
c(
  adaboost = auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_ada),
  logit = auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_logit),
  tree4 = auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_tree),
  rf = auroc(df_holz$replicate, y_rf)
) |>
  round(3)
```

## Selecting versus Evaluating

Listing 34 scores every setting in the hypergrid on the six tuning projects, and we took the row with the most stable performance. I think that this number is not an estimate of how the chosen model will do on a new project, because the same six projects picked the winner and then graded it. To see how much that matters, we should do the selection where the project we want to score cannot influence it.

## Addition: Nested LOGO-CV

Setting a project aside costs data: HOLZ's 26 studies never helped choose the
setting, and the final test in Listing 35 rests on those 26 studies alone.
Nested LOGO-CV avoids both. It repeats the whole procedure -- search the grid,
pick the winner, refit it -- once per project, each time with that project held
out. Every project serves as the test once, and none is withheld from tuning for
good. The result estimates the procedure, not any single setting, and it shows
which setting each search chose, so you see how stable the choice is. It is
worth its cost, one grid search per project, when the data are too few to spare
a test project, or when the stability of the choice is itself the question.

::: {.callout-note}
## Nested LOGO-CV picks by the mean

`logo_cv(nested = TRUE)` lets each inner search pick the setting with the
highest mean AUROC (`criterion = "auroc"`), not the highest mean minus SD that
Listing 34 uses. Listing 36 ranks by the mean as well, so its two versions agree
with each other, but not with the stability rule of the main thread. To nest
that rule, rank the inner settings by mean minus SD inside the loop of
Listing 36.
:::

In nested leave-one-group-out cross-validation, the outer loop holds
out one project entirely and the inner loop repeats the whole grid search on the six that remain, choosing hyperparameters without ever seeing the held-out project. The
chosen setting is then refit on those six projects and scored on the seventh.
Repeat seven times.

When I first met Nested LOGO-CV, I had a hard time to wrap my head around the fact, that it does not give me a(n overall) performance estimate for a particular hyperparameter setting. 
Instead, it puts a number (an estimate) on the procedure: "run the grid search, pick, then fit the winner." Every model built inside the nesting is discarded; none of them is the model you ship. You still fit one setting on all the projects you have. Nesting tells you what to expect from that
model, not what it scores.

completely separating the tuning process from the evaluation process

if you have a very large training validation and test set you can do the tripple, but if you have very vew data (as we comparably do) we might consider moving to nested cross-validation.

Take our data and split it into folds (the 5 groups in our case). Then we reserve one group, say Group 1, as test set (let's call this the outer test set). 
Then we take the remaining 4 (Group 2, 3, 4, 5) and split them again into 4 pieces: 3 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4) for the training set and one for the (inner) test set (Group 5). Then we (randomly, we do full Cartesian) search a hyperparameter setting from our test set and train the model with the inner 3 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4) and score it on the inner test set (Group 5) - and then again with a different hyperparameter setting. Then, we select the winning model with the best hyperparameter combi on Group 5 and pass it to the outer loop and train the model using the bigger training set with 4 pieces (Group 2, 3, 4, 5) and then evaluate it on the outer test set (Group 1). And then you repeat the whole procedure again with the next group
So instead of one model performance on on test set we have 5 (5 Groups) measures. What people than usually do is to take the mean performance across projects.
So we use all the data as a test set once

In small test set you can have the problem of bad luck and up (especially with small test sets) with a handy partition which is too easy to classify and (thus not representative of what would usually happen, i.e. performane overestimate).

TODO: Random grid search. Define 20 as a number in the random search

Two things follow. First, the seven inner searches may each select a different
setting, and the setting that won in Listing 34 may be chosen by none of them.
That is expected rather than alarming: with seven projects there is no stable
"best" setting to find, and seeing that instability directly is more informative
than the average that hides it. Second, the nested estimate is *conservative*
here, because each nested model saw six projects while a model fitted on all of
them sees seven.

If nesting does not hand you a model, what does? The three listings have three
different jobs, and it is worth being explicit about which is which:

| job | listing |
|:----|:--------|
| Choose the hyperparameters, using the six tuning projects | Listing 34 |
| Estimate what that choice is worth, on one held-out project | Listing 35 |
| Estimate what the choosing procedure is worth, with every project held out once | Listing 36 |

So Listing 34 still picks the setting and Listing 35 still tests it -- nesting
changes neither. What it adds is a number for the whole procedure: not the
winning score from Listing 34, which the same six projects produced by selecting
it, and not a single test project, but an estimate from every project, none of
which had a hand in choosing its own setting.

The settings the inner searches picked are worth looking at, but they are a
diagnostic rather than a shortlist. They have the same standing as the
coefficients fitted inside each cross-validation fold back in Module 1: nobody
averages those, and nobody asks which fold's coefficients to keep. They are
by-products of a procedure being measured, not candidates for shipping.

#### Listing 36

Code to do a nested leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

::: {.callout-note}
This ran for approximately 10 minutes on our laptops.
:::

```{r listing-36}
# Projects, in the order they take their turn: all seven, HOLZ included
projects <- sort(unique(df$pid))

# Partition data by project ID
df_split <- split(df, df$pid)

# One honest score and one selected setting per project
nested_auc <- list()
selected <- list()

runtime <- system.time({
  # OUTER loop: evaluates
  for (rp in projects) {
    # Progress report
    message("\nOuter fold: ", rp, "\n")

    # Training and test set. The test project leaves the data entirely, so
    # nothing below can see it.
    test <- df_split[[rp]]
    train <- df[!(df$pid %in% rp), ]

    # INNER loop: selects. This is the same grid search as Listing 34, run on
    # the training projects only -- so we can hand it to logo_cv().
    inner <- logo_cv(
      replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o,
      data = train,
      group = "pid",
      grid = hgrid[, c("depth", "T", "eta")]
    )

    # Rank the settings by their mean over the inner folds. Here the mean is a
    # ranking device, not a performance estimate.
    inner_auc <- summary(inner, metric = "auroc")
    ranked <- aggregate(estimate ~ setting, data = inner_auc, FUN = mean)

    # The setting the six training projects chose, on their own
    inner_best <- hgrid[ranked$setting[which.max(ranked$estimate)], ]
    selected[[rp]] <- inner_best[, c("depth", "T", "eta")]

    # Refit at that setting and score the untouched project
    h <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train[, voi_nms],
      maxdepth = inner_best$depth,
      model = TRUE
    )
    fit <- adaboost(
      h,
      n_iter = inner_best$T,
      eta = inner_best$eta,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
    y_pred <- predict(
      fit,
      newdata = test[, pred_nms],
      type = "margin",
      verbose = FALSE
    )
    nested_auc[[rp]] <- auroc(test$replicate, y_pred)
  }
})

# Waiting time
message("Run time: ", runtime["elapsed"], " s\n")

# The honest expectation, per project
unlist(nested_auc)

# What each outer fold selected, and how often they disagree
do.call(rbind, selected)
```

Only the outer loop is new. The inner one is the leave-one-group-out search we
already ran in Listing 34, so we hand it to `logo_cv()` rather than write it out
again -- the single change is that it now sees `train` instead of `df_noholz`.

The whole procedure is also one call:

```{r listing-36-oneline}
nested <- logo_cv(
  replicate ~ power.o + effect_size.o + n.o + p_value.o,
  data = df,
  group = "pid",
  grid = hgrid[, c("depth", "T", "eta")],
  nested = TRUE,
  criterion = "auroc"
)
nested
```
